rv.q: On a second viewing, Steel’s portrait of a working-class community in red wall Nottinghamshire, immaculately directed by Bijan Sheibani (who set out his crowd control credentials in Barber Shop Chronicles), looks even more of a modern classic.
It’s still an early contender for the best play of the year.
Beth Steel’s wonderfully Chekhovian drama about a fateful East Midlands wedding is even better as it hits the West End.
It remains a manifestly riveting evening, a testament to the actors’ ability to invest larger-than-life ebullience with truthfulness, and to the subject matter’s rare immediacy.
Steel’s script is sharply observed and often very funny, enlivened by spikily natural dialogue.
The strength of individual characterisations elevates the drama from a mere cacophony of raw emotions, and is further supplemented by an unending stream of hilariously dumped one-liners.
Director Bijan Sheibani steers this ensemble through the play’s patches of chaos and pathos with exemplary control.
A wild, messy and beautiful piece of theatre.
Carol is worth the price of a ticket to this show by herself.
This is a production that crackles with authenticity, humour, and heartbreak; a richly textured portrait of a working-class family on the edge of transformation.

cn.t: Critics widely praise Beth Steel's working-class wedding drama for its raw authenticity, stellar ensemble, and Chekhovian blend of comedy and heartbreak. A triumphant West End transfer.

vr.q: One of the best plays that you could see this summer in London.
